title: How We Know: Detecting a Signal

generated.pipeline: extract → Gemini draft → Claude Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In biochemical signaling, causal claims earn belief when two methods that {{c1::fail differently}} agree.
cards.why: Every detection method has blind spots, so agreement across methods with different failure modes strengthens causal evidence.
cards.quote: Competition, antibodies, and mass spectrometry detect scarce signals, each with blind spots; causal claims earn belief when two methods that fail differently agree.

cards.front: A radioimmunoassay measures a scarce hormone by letting unlabelled sample hormone compete with a fixed radiolabelled tracer for a fixed, {{c1::limiting}} amount of antibody.
cards.why: Bound and free label are then separated and the concentration is read against known standards.
cards.quote: letting unlabelled sample hormone compete with a fixed radiolabelled tracer for a fixed, limiting amount of antibody
cards.section: Measuring almost nothing: let the hormone compete with a labelled copy

cards.front: In a radioimmunoassay, how does antibody-bound radioactivity change as unlabelled hormone in the sample increases, and why?
cards.back: Bound radioactivity falls because unlabelled hormone from the sample competes with the fixed radiolabelled tracer for the limited antibody binding sites.
cards.quote: letting unlabelled sample hormone compete with a fixed radiolabelled tracer for a fixed, limiting amount of antibody
cards.section: Measuring almost nothing: let the hormone compete with a labelled copy

cards.front: Why must the antibody binding sites in a radioimmunoassay be fewer than the radiolabelled hormone molecules?
cards.back: If antibody sites were not limiting, every labelled molecule would find a site and a small amount of unlabelled sample hormone would barely change the bound count.
cards.quote: The antibody sites must be limiting, fewer than the labelled hormone molecules, or every labelled molecule would find a site
cards.section: Measuring almost nothing: let the hormone compete with a labelled copy

cards.front: Why do real radioimmunoassays read unknown hormone levels from an empirical standard curve instead of relying only on the high-affinity saturation limit?
cards.back: Affinity and concentration rarely keep antibody sites completely full across the whole measurement range, so unknowns must be read against known standards.
cards.quote: Because affinity and concentration rarely keep sites completely full across the whole range, real assays always read unknowns against an empirical standard curve
cards.section: Measuring almost nothing: let the hormone compete with a labelled copy

cards.front: In an insulin radioimmunoassay with fixed antibody and tracer, 0 pM unlabelled insulin gives 8,000 cpm bound, while standards of 15, 45, and 135 pM leave 6,000, 4,000, and 2,000 cpm bound. A plasma sample mixed with two equal volumes of buffer (a 1:3 dilution) leaves 4,000 cpm bound. What is the insulin concentration in the undiluted plasma?
cards.back: 135 pM. The diluted sample gives 4,000 cpm bound, matching the 45 pM standard. Because mixing 1 volume of plasma with 2 volumes of buffer diluted it 3-fold, undiluted insulin = 45 pM × 3 = 135 pM.
cards.quote: separating bound from free label and reading the concentration off known standards.
cards.section: Measuring almost nothing: let the hormone compete with a labelled copy

cards.front: In the high-affinity saturation limit of a radioimmunoassay, bound label tracks tracer divided by total hormone. If a tube holds 20 pM radiolabelled hormone and yields 6,000 cpm bound with no sample, what bound radioactivity is expected when 60 pM unlabelled hormone is added?
cards.back: 1,500 cpm. Total hormone = 20 pM + 60 pM = 80 pM. Bound label scales by tracer / total hormone = 20 / 80 = 0.25, giving 6,000 cpm × 0.25 = 1,500 cpm.
cards.quote: The first film showed the high-affinity saturation limit, where bound label tracks tracer divided by total hormone.
cards.section: Measuring almost nothing: let the hormone compete with a labelled copy

cards.front: A blood sample contains a biologically inactive hormone fragment that keeps the short surface the assay antibody recognises. What happens in a radioimmunoassay, and will it agree with a bioassay?
cards.back: The radioimmunoassay detects the fragment as hormone (lowering bound radioactivity) and disagrees with a bioassay. Radioimmunoassays count whatever surface the antibody binds, whereas bioassays measure biological activity.
cards.quote: Bioassays (finding a signal) measure what a hormone does; a radioimmunoassay counts what the antibody recognises, which is usually, but not always, active hormone.
cards.section: Measuring almost nothing: let the hormone compete with a labelled copy

cards.front: In SDS-PAGE, heating a cell extract in SDS unfolds each protein and coats it with negative charge roughly in proportion to {{c1::length}}, so an electric field pulls smaller proteins farther.
cards.quote: heating the extract in SDS unfolds each protein and coats it with negative charge roughly in proportion to length, so an electric field pulls smaller proteins farther
cards.section: Seeing one protein among thousands: sort by size, then ask an antibody

cards.front: In a western blot, after transferring sorted bands to a membrane and adding an antibody to the target protein, detection uses a second {{c1::enzyme-linked antibody}} that makes light or colour.
cards.quote: add an antibody to your protein, then a second enzyme-linked antibody that makes light or colour, giving a band at one size.
cards.section: Seeing one protein among thousands: sort by size, then ask an antibody

cards.front: A {{c1::phosphospecific antibody}}, raised against a short phosphorylated peptide, is chosen to bind only when that specific phosphate is present.
cards.why: It reads one known phosphorylation site minutes after a signal arrives.
cards.quote: A phosphospecific antibody, raised against a short phosphorylated peptide and chosen to bind only when that phosphate is present, reads one known site minutes after a signal arrives.
cards.section: Seeing one protein among thousands: sort by size, then ask an antibody

cards.front: How do SDS-PAGE and immunoprecipitation treat protein structure in opposite ways?
cards.back: SDS-PAGE heats extracts in SDS to unfold proteins and sort them by size, whereas immunoprecipitation uses an unheated, native extract to pull out a target with bound partners.
cards.quote: Immunoprecipitation fishes from an unheated, native extract: an antibody on beads pulls out its target together with bound partners.
cards.section: Seeing one protein among thousands: sort by size, then ask an antibody

cards.front: Why must a co-immunoprecipitation include a parallel tube with an unrelated antibody?
cards.back: It rules out non-specific sticking of the target or partner protein to the beads rather than true association with the immunoprecipitated protein.
cards.quote: a parallel tube with an unrelated antibody rules out sticking to the beads.
cards.section: Seeing one protein among thousands: sort by size, then ask an antibody

cards.front: When a phosphospecific western blot shows a darker band after stimulation, why must you also blot the same samples for total protein?
cards.back: Without a total-protein blot, you cannot distinguish more phosphate per protein molecule from a larger amount of the protein itself.
cards.quote: Always blot the same samples for total protein too, or you cannot tell more phosphate per molecule from more protein.
cards.section: Seeing one protein among thousands: sort by size, then ask an antibody

cards.front: To test whether protein A binds protein B by immunoprecipitating A, you heat the cell extract in SDS first. What happens, and why?
cards.back: The interaction is missed and protein B stays behind. Heat and SDS unfold proteins and break non-covalent interactions, separating A from B before the antibody beads capture A.
cards.quote: SDS and heat unfold the proteins and break non-covalent interactions, separating A from B before the beads touch them.
cards.section: Seeing one protein among thousands: sort by size, then ask an antibody

cards.front: A phosphospecific western blot shows a much darker band after hormone treatment while total protein stays unchanged. Can you conclude that most molecules of the protein carry phosphate, and what control checks antibody specificity?
cards.back: No; a darker band does not show what fraction of molecules carry phosphate. You also need a sample lacking the protein or that phosphate to rule out binding the wrong protein.
cards.quote: a darker band does not tell you what fraction of molecules carry phosphate; antibodies can bind the wrong protein
cards.section: Seeing one protein among thousands: sort by size, then ask an antibody

cards.front: A patient's blood gives a high hormone reading in a radioimmunoassay but weak activity in a bioassay, suggesting a cleaved, inactive fragment that retains the antibody's binding surface. How could SDS-PAGE and a western blot with the same antibody test this?
cards.back: Run the blood sample alongside intact hormone on SDS-PAGE and blot with the antibody; a cleaved fragment migrates farther and produces a smaller-size band than intact hormone. This rests on the rules that radioimmunoassays count antibody-recognised surfaces regardless of activity while SDS-PAGE sorts unfolded proteins by length.
cards.quote: heating the extract in SDS unfolds each protein and coats it with negative charge roughly in proportion to length
cards.section: Seeing one protein among thousands: sort by size, then ask an antibody

cards.front: In mass spectrometry, the mass of a phosphopeptide equals the mass of the unmodified peptide plus about {{c1::80 daltons}} for each phosphate.
cards.quote: mass of a phosphopeptide = mass of the peptide + about 80 daltons for each phosphate
cards.section: Where is the protein modified? Weigh the pieces

cards.front: Before mass spectrometry, trypsin cuts a protein into peptides after {{c1::lysine and arginine}}, usually not before proline.
cards.quote: Mass spectrometry cuts the protein into peptides with trypsin (after lysine and arginine, usually not before proline)
cards.section: Where is the protein modified? Weigh the pieces

cards.front: How does tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) pinpoint which residue carries a phosphate, and when does localization stay ambiguous?
cards.back: MS/MS breaks one peptide's backbone and tracks the extra ~80 daltons across sequenced fragments; if no cut falls between candidate residues, localization narrows only to two or three residues.
cards.quote: those carrying the extra 80 daltons pinpoint the residue—provided cuts fall between candidate residues; otherwise the site narrows only to two or three residues.
cards.section: Where is the protein modified? Weigh the pieces

cards.front: Once mass spectrometry locates a newly phosphorylated residue after a signal arrives, what two causal questions remain open?
cards.back: It does not tell you which of the cell's roughly five hundred kinases added the phosphate, nor whether that step causes the response.
cards.quote: Locating a phosphate shows what changed, not which of the cell's roughly five hundred kinases put it there or whether that step causes the response.
cards.section: Where is the protein modified? Weigh the pieces

cards.front: An unphosphorylated tryptic peptide has a mass of 1,320.6 Da. After stimulation, mass spectrometry detects the same peptide at 1,480.6 Da. How many phosphates were added, and what mass would the singly phosphorylated form have?
cards.back: 2 phosphates; singly phosphorylated mass is about 1,400.6 Da. Mass shift = 1,480.6 − 1,320.6 = 160.0 Da, so 160.0 / 80 = 2 phosphates. Adding one phosphate gives 1,320.6 + 80 = 1,400.6 Da.
cards.quote: mass of a phosphopeptide = mass of the peptide + about 80 daltons for each phosphate
cards.section: Where is the protein modified? Weigh the pieces

cards.front: A whole-extract MS/MS screen reports two thousand phosphorylation sites after stimulation, but a suspected site on protein Q is missing. Does this prove the site is unphosphorylated, and why?
cards.back: No; the site may still be phosphorylated. Some peptides are never detected because of cleavage, enrichment, ionisation, or fragmentation, so an unreported site is not proof of absence.
cards.quote: Some peptides are never detected because of cleavage, enrichment, ionisation or fragmentation, so an unreported site may still exist.
cards.section: Where is the protein modified? Weigh the pieces

cards.front: A phosphospecific blot against Ser30 of protein P shows no change after stimulation, and you want to check for unknown phosphorylation sites elsewhere on P. Why does phosphopeptide-enriched MS/MS overcome the blot's blind spot, and what happens if no MS/MS backbone cut falls between two adjacent serines?
cards.back: Antibody blots cannot discover unsuspected sites, whereas enriched MS/MS needs no prior guess and spots ~80 dalton shifts across peptides. If no backbone cut falls between two adjacent serines, MS/MS narrows the phosphate only to that pair rather than one residue. This rests on the antibody blind-spot rule and the MS/MS fragmentation rule.
cards.quote: After enriching rare phosphopeptides, one run on a whole extract can report thousands of sites with no prior guess.
cards.section: Where is the protein modified? Weigh the pieces

cards.front: Replacing the bulky {{c1::gatekeeper}} residue in a kinase's shared ATP pocket with glycine or alanine opens a hole, creating an analog-sensitive kinase.
cards.quote: In the shared ATP pocket, a bulky gatekeeper residue limits what fits; replacing it with glycine or alanine opens a hole, making an analog-sensitive kinase.
cards.section: Which kinase? Give one kinase an ATP of its own

cards.front: Why does an ATP analog with a benzyl group on its adenine and a radioactive gamma phosphate selectively label direct substrate candidates of an analog-sensitive kinase?
cards.back: The bulky benzyl group fits normal kinase pockets poorly, so only the enlarged pocket accepts the analog and transfers the radioactive gamma phosphate to its direct substrates.
cards.quote: An ATP analog with a bulky benzyl group on its adenine fits this enlarged pocket and fits normal kinases poorly.
cards.section: Which kinase? Give one kinase an ATP of its own

cards.front: A purified kinase phosphorylates protein Y in a test tube, and the same kinase co-immunoprecipitates with protein Z from cell extracts. Why does neither result prove a direct substrate in cells?
cards.back: Neither proves an in-cell direct substrate. Test tubes use high concentrations without cellular scaffolds or compartments (showing only what the kinase can phosphorylate), while co-immunoprecipitation shows binding contact, not catalysis.
cards.quote: concentrations are high and the cell's scaffolds and compartments are gone. Finding the kinase bound to a protein shows contact, which is not catalysis.
cards.section: Which kinase? Give one kinase an ATP of its own

cards.front: MS/MS finds a ~80 Da shift at Ser210 of protein R after stimulation, and a sequence motif tool predicts kinase K acts there. Why does neither prove K directly phosphorylates R in cells, and how does an analog-sensitive K assay address the gap?
cards.back: Sequence tools give only candidates, and MS/MS locates a phosphate without identifying which of ~500 kinases added it. Mutating K's gatekeeper to glycine or alanine lets only engineered K transfer radioactive gamma phosphate from a benzyl-ATP analog, identifying direct substrate candidates. This rests on the prediction/MS/MS attribution limits and the enlarged-pocket selectivity rule.
cards.quote: Because the bulky group stays on adenine and only the radioactive gamma phosphate transfers, labelled proteins are candidates for direct substrates of that kinase.
cards.section: Which kinase? Give one kinase an ATP of its own

cards.front: Most small-molecule kinase inhibitors hit off-target enzymes because they plug the {{c1::ATP pocket}} shared by about five hundred kinases.
cards.quote: Most kinase inhibitors plug the ATP pocket shared by about five hundred kinases.
cards.section: What an inhibitor proves, and what "necessary" and "sufficient" mean

cards.front: Mutating a phosphorylation site to {{c1::alanine}} tests whether phosphorylation is necessary, because it has no hydroxyl group to accept phosphate.
cards.quote: A step is necessary if removing it removes the response: a knockout, controlled inhibitor, or mutating the site to alanine (no hydroxyl to accept phosphate).
cards.section: What an inhibitor proves, and what "necessary" and "sufficient" mean

cards.front: A signaling step is {{c1::sufficient}} if turning it on alone triggers the response without the signal.
cards.why: Examples include an always-active kinase or—more weakly—mutating a phosphorylation site to aspartate.
cards.quote: A step is sufficient if turning it on alone triggers the response without the signal: an always-active kinase, or—more weakly—mutating the site to aspartate
cards.section: What an inhibitor proves, and what "necessary" and "sufficient" mean

cards.front: Why is the causal logic of an unselective kinase inhibitor one-sided?
cards.back: If shutting off kinase X leaves the response intact, X is ruled out as unnecessary; if the response stops, either X or an off-target kinase could be responsible.
cards.quote: if shutting off kinase X leaves the response intact, X is not needed; if the response stops, X or any off-target may be responsible.
cards.section: What an inhibitor proves, and what "necessary" and "sufficient" mean

cards.front: Two structurally unrelated inhibitors both block kinase X in vitro and both stop a hormone response in cells. Why is this stronger than doubling one inhibitor's dose, and what could still mislead you?
cards.back: Unlike structures rarely share the same off-targets, whereas doubling one dose only widens its off-target list. Shared off-targets still remain possible, so a drug-resistant mutant of X plus independent genetics is cleaner.
cards.quote: Doubling one dose only widens its off-target list, whereas unlike structures rarely share the same off-targets.
cards.section: What an inhibitor proves, and what "necessary" and "sufficient" mean

cards.front: Inhibitor C blocks kinase K plus eleven other kinases in cells and prevents phosphorylation of protein S. When cells express an active, C-resistant mutant of K in place of normal K, inhibitor C no longer blocks S phosphorylation. What does this prove, and what does it not prove?
cards.back: It proves inhibitor C acted through K (so K is necessary), because the off-target kinases remained blocked while S phosphorylation returned. It does not prove pathway order, a direct link, or sufficiency.
cards.quote: Expressing a drug-resistant mutant of X sharpens the proof: if the response returns while other targets stay blocked, the drug acted through X.
cards.section: What an inhibitor proves, and what "necessary" and "sufficient" mean

cards.front: Expressing an always-active mutant of kinase M triggers a cellular response without any hormone. What does this prove, and does it show that M is needed for the hormone's normal response?
cards.back: It proves that kinase M activity is sufficient to trigger the response, but it does not prove M is necessary for the hormone's normal response; a step can be sufficient without being necessary.
cards.quote: an always-active kinase, or—more weakly—mutating the site to aspartate, which mimics phosphate only in part. A step can be one without the other.
cards.section: What an inhibitor proves, and what "necessary" and "sufficient" mean

cards.front: Inhibitor Z blocks kinase K and nine off-target kinases, weakening the phosphospecific blot band for substrate S after insulin. What two controls—one for the blot readout and one for inhibitor specificity—are needed to show K is necessary for insulin-stimulated S phosphorylation?
cards.back: Blot the same samples for total S to confirm less phosphate per molecule rather than less S protein, and express a Z-resistant mutant of K (or add independent genetics) so you know Z acted through K while off-targets stayed blocked. This rests on the total-protein blot rule and the drug-resistant rescue rule.
cards.quote: Adding genetics—a knockout or knockdown—tests the claim with a method that fails differently.
cards.section: What an inhibitor proves, and what "necessary" and "sufficient" mean

cards.front: Mutating Ser50 of protein T to alanine blocks a hormone response, mutating Ser50 to aspartate gives no response without hormone, and an always-active upstream kinase K triggers the response without hormone. What does this combination prove and leave unproven?
cards.back: Ser50 phosphorylation is necessary (alanine removes the response) and K activity is sufficient (always-active K triggers it without hormone). The silent aspartate mutant does not rule out Ser50 sufficiency because aspartate mimics phosphate only in part, and always-active K does not prove K is necessary. This rests on the necessity/sufficiency rules and the partial-mimic limit.
cards.quote: A step is necessary if removing it removes the response: a knockout, controlled inhibitor, or mutating the site to alanine (no hydroxyl to accept phosphate).
cards.section: What an inhibitor proves, and what "necessary" and "sufficient" mean

cards.front: Why cannot adding ordinary radioactive ATP to a cell extract identify the direct substrates of one kinase?
cards.back: Every active kinase in the extract uses ordinary ATP, labelling substrates of all active kinases at once with nothing marking which kinase transferred each phosphate.
cards.quote: Every kinase in the extract uses ordinary ATP, so radioactive ATP labels the substrates of every active kinase at once.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In an analog-sensitive kinase substrate screen using N6-benzyl radioactive ATP in a cell extract, what negative control must you run, and how do you handle a band that appears there?
cards.back: Run the same extract with the normal kinase in place of the mutant, which should yield no labelled bands. Any band appearing there comes from a kinase using the analog unaided and is discarded.
cards.quote: The control is the same extract with the normal kinase in place of the mutant. It should give no labelled bands.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: After an analog-sensitive gatekeeper mutant of kinase K labels protein V in a cell extract (with no band in the wild-type control), how can the same engineered kinase test whether K is necessary for V phosphorylation in living cells, and why pair it with a knockout or knockdown?
cards.back: Use a bulky inhibitor built for the enlarged gatekeeper pocket in cells expressing mutant K—shutting off mutant K while sparing normal kinases—and check V phosphorylation. Pair it with a knockout or knockdown so two methods that fail differently agree. This rests on the bulky-inhibitor specificity rule and the converging-methods rule.
cards.quote: The enlarged pocket helps there too: a bulky inhibitor built for it shuts off the mutant kinase and spares the normal ones.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Yalow and Berson injected radioactive iodine-tagged insulin expecting faster destruction in diabetic patients, yet radioactivity left the blood more slowly in insulin-treated patients and migrated with serum globulins on paper electrophoresis. What did this reveal?
cards.back: Previously treated patients had serum antibodies (globulins) that bound the injected insulin and held it in the blood, overturning doubts that a 51-amino-acid protein could raise antibodies.
cards.quote: When their serum was sorted by paper electrophoresis, the radioactivity travelled with a globulin, the class of serum protein that includes antibodies.
cards.section: How the insulin antibody was found

cards.front: In the BATF transcription factor study, endogenous BATF ran on a gel as shifted bands that disappeared after treatment with calf intestinal alkaline phosphatase. What did this show?
cards.back: It showed that BATF is phosphorylated in vivo, because enzymatic removal of phosphate groups eliminated the gel mobility shift.
cards.quote: BATF from cells ran on a gel as shifted bands that calf intestinal alkaline phosphatase removed, which showed phosphorylation in vivo.
cards.section: A worked case: BATF

cards.front: Why is mutating a serine phosphorylation site to aspartate only an imperfect phosphomimetic?
cards.back: Aspartate carries less negative charge than a phosphate group and has a different shape, so a mutant that does nothing is weak evidence.
cards.quote: Such phosphomimetic mutants are imperfect: aspartate carries less charge than a phosphate and has a different shape, so a mutant that does nothing is weak evidence.
cards.section: A worked case: BATF

cards.front: When Karaman, Zarrinkar, and colleagues tested 38 kinase inhibitors against 317 kinases, what general conclusion did they reach about measuring inhibitor selectivity?
cards.back: They concluded that small assay panels do not provide a robust measure of selectivity.
cards.quote: measured thirty-eight inhibitors against 317 kinases and concluded that "small assay panels do not provide a robust measure of selectivity."
cards.section: The inhibitor surveys
